<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The Transformer architecture has achieved significant success in natural language processing, motivating its adaptation to computer vision tasks.
Unlike convolutional neural networks, vision transformers inherently capture long-range dependencies and enable parallel processing, yet lack inductive biases and efficiency benefits, facing significant computational and memory challenges that limit its real-world applicability.
This paper surveys various online strategies for generating lightweight vision transformers for image recognition, focusing on three key areas: <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Component Design</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Network</span>, and <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge Distillation</span>.
We evaluate the relevant exploration for each topic on the ImageNet-1K benchmark, analyzing trade-offs among precision, parameters, throughput, and more to highlight their respective advantages, disadvantages, and flexibility.
Finally, we propose future research directions and potential challenges in the lightweighting of vision transformers with the aim of inspiring further exploration and providing practical guidance for the community.
Project Page: <a href="https://github.com/ajxklo/Lightweight-VIT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ajxklo/Lightweight-VIT</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Model Lightweight, Vision Transformer, Image Recognition, Model Compression, Computer Vision
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Introduction</span></h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/picture/n5.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/71;" width="476" height="71" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1. </span>
<span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ViT Lightweighting Overview.</span>
We categorize existing techniques for alleviating the computational burden of ViT into two steps: online lightweighting and offline lightweighting. <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a)</annotation></semantics></math> Online lightweighting techniques reduce the computational burden during training while ensuring the model structure or expressive capability is kept complete in a soft manner; <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b)</annotation></semantics></math> Offline lightweighting techniques, such as pruning and quantization, trim unnecessary capacity from the model structure. In this paper, we focus more on online lightweighting techniques.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Vision Transformer (ViT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khan et al., 2022</a>)</cite> rapidly emerge as powerful tools for image recognition, challenging the dominance of the traditional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. Using the self-attention mechanism of transformers in natural language processing, ViT models encode images as sequences of patches, allowing them to effectively capture global dependencies and contextual information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, yielding remarkable performance improvements in various vision tasks, including image generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hatamizadeh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey and Singh, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Torbunov et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marnissi and Fathallah, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boukerche and Hou, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Antonelli et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amjoud and Amrouch, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gehrig and Scaramuzza, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, Embodied Artificial Intelligence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and semantic segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thisanke et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ando et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
In addition, ViT models show remarkable precision in conventional image recognition benchmarks, achieving near-perfect validation results, such as surpassing an impressive precision <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math> on the CIFAR-10 dataset.
Consequently, the limitations of small-scale datasets in fully demonstrating the performance superiority of ViT models lead to a shift towards larger benchmark datasets like ImageNet-1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> for evaluating recognition tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/m8.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/256;" width="476" height="256" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2. </span><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Online ViT Lightweighting Overview.</span>
The general overview diagram of this paper shows the basic structure of the paper at the top, and at the bottom lists the methods collated in this paper regarding the online lightweighting of ViT models, mainly efficient ViT components, dynamic networks and knowledge distillation methods.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite ViT models impressive performance,  they have significant drawbacks in model size and computational overhead. The increased parameters and complex operations slow training and inference and increase resource consumption, limiting practical deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tabani et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
To address these issues, a variety of lightweighting techniques are proposed, aiming to reduce the computational burden without substantially compromising model performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This survey focuses on online lightweighting strategies<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fournier et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tay et al., 2022</a>)</cite> for ViT models, which differ from offline post-processing methods such as pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu and Xiang, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu and Wu, 2023</a>)</cite> and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Online techniques aim to optimize the model during training, either by improving the design of internal components <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, transferring knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, or dynamically adjusting the computational path of the network based on the complexity of the input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. The goal is to achieve a “<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">soft</span>" lightweighting, maintaining the model architecture and expressive capacity while enhancing efficiency. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, online lightweighting techniques are seen as a precursor to more aggressive offline post-processing methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We categorize online lightweighting techniques for ViT models into three main topics: efficient component design, dynamic network, and knowledge distillation (KD).
These topics exploit the ViT property on token-based input to achieve unique efficiency gains.
For example, token input updates can be handled using native self-attention, refined linear attention, or even attention-free <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Buoy et al., 2023</a>)</cite> mechanisms.
To address spatial redundancy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, dynamic token pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and token merging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng and Zhang, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> strategies are used, offering a more granular approach compared to traditional downsampling of CNN models.
Integrating these techniques allows for customized, lightweight strategies developed for real-world applications.
Our contributions in this survey are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comprehensive Overview</span>. We provide a broad survey of online lightweighting techniques for vision transformer, distinguishing them from offline post-processing techniques, and categorize them into three key topics: efficient component design, dynamic network, and knowledge distillation, with each topic discussed in the context of input flow forwarding.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trade-Off Presentation.</span> Using ImageNet-1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> as the benchmark, we present a detailed analysis of the trade-offs between precision and efficiency for various online lightweighting strategies, offering both qualitative and quantitative insights.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Future Directions</span>.
We identify the limitations of current online lightweighting techniques, highlight common assumptions that may need reconsideration, and propose promising research directions, including privacy-sensitive models.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

<td id="S1.T1.2.1.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;"><math id="S1.T1.m1" class="ltx_Math" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;" mathbackground="#E6E6E6" mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S1.T1.2.1.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S1.T1.2.1.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;">Query Matrix</td>
<td id="S1.T1.2.1.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;">Value Matrix</td>
<td id="S1.T1.2.1.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;">Key Matrix</td>
<td id="S1.T1.2.1.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;">Embedding Dimension</td>
<td id="S1.T1.2.1.10.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1.65pt;padding-bottom:1.65pt;">Computation Complexity</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Difference from Other Surveys</span> This survey focuses mainly on online lightweighting techniques of ViT models and provides comprehensive experimental reports to uniformly examine the trade-offs existing strategies make between precision and efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Survey Overview</span>
This survey uses simplified notation from Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the structure: Section <a href="#S2" title="2. Original ViT Pipeline ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> introduces the vision transformer concept and pipeline. We then present online lightweight strategies on three main topics.
The first topic, discussed in Section <a href="#S3" title="3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, explores the <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">efficient component</span> design within ViT.
The second topic, presented in Section <a href="#S4" title="4. Dynamic Network ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, explores <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dynamic networks</span> based on input complexity, including dynamic resolution and depth adaptation.
The third topic, in Section <a href="#S5" title="5. Knowledge Distillation ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, focuses on the use of the unique advantages of ViT for <span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">knowledge distillation</span>.
For each topic, we report from a unified perspective on the results of image recognition performance evaluations on the ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> benchmark for the methods involved, analyzing their advantages and disadvantages, as well as flexibility.
Finally, in Section <a href="#S6" title="6. Future Research Directions ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we offer a discussion on promising directions for future exploration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Original ViT Pipeline</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2. Original ViT Pipeline ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, given an input image <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> with resolution <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\times W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\times W</annotation></semantics></math>, the first step in the ViT pipeline involves dividing the image into non-overlapping <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=(H/P)\times(W/P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=(H/P)\times(W/P)</annotation></semantics></math> patches, each of size <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\times P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\times P</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> represents the patch size. Each patch <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times P\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times P\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> undergoes a flattening operation to obtain a linear embedding <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{P^{2}C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{P^{2}C}</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by a linear projection to obtain the patch embedding <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{p}^{0}=\mathbf{E}\mathbf{x}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐄𝐱</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{p}^{0}=\mathbf{E}\mathbf{x}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times P^{2}C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times P^{2}C}</annotation></semantics></math> is a learnable projection matrix and <math id="S2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is the embedding dimension.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To incorporate positional information, a positional embedding <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{E}_{pos}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{E}_{pos}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times D}</annotation></semantics></math> is added to the patch embeddings. The resulting sequence of embedded patches <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{0}=[\mathbf{z}_{cls};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{0};\ldots;\mathbf{z}_{N}^{0}]+\mathbf{E}_{pos}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{0}=[\mathbf{z}_{cls};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{0};\ldots;\mathbf{z}_{N}^{0}]+\mathbf{E}_{pos}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the input to the transformer encoder, where <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}</annotation></semantics></math> is a learnable [CLS] token that facilitates recognition.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The transformer encoder consists of <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> layers, each comprising a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) block, a Feed-Forward Network (FFN) or Multilayer Perceptron (MLP).
In the MHSA block, the input sequence <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly projected to obtain the query <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐐</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, key <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐊</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{K}</annotation></semantics></math> and value <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐕</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}</annotation></semantics></math> using the learned projection matrices <math id="S2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{q},\mathbf{W}_{k},\mathbf{W}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{h}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{q},\mathbf{W}_{k},\mathbf{W}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{h}}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. The attention weights are computed as <math id="S2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V})=\text{softmax}(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{T}}{\sqrt{D_{h}}})\mathbf{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Attention</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐊</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐕</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>𝐐𝐊</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msqrt><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></msqrt></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐕</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V})=\text{softmax}(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{T}}{\sqrt{D_{h}}})\mathbf{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{h}</annotation></semantics></math> is the dimension of each head. The outputs of the <math id="S2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> attention heads are concatenated and linearly projected using <math id="S2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{HD_{h}\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{HD_{h}\times D}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain the MSA output.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/m9.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/171;" width="476" height="171" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3. </span><span id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Original ViT Overview.</span>
The pipeline of the original ViT for image recognition is divided into four main components. Firstly, Patch Embedding is used to obtain input in token form. Secondly, there is a stack of Transformer layers, which includes the Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) mechanism, facilitating ViT global comprehension ability. Finally, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) structure is employed to project into category space.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The FFN consists of two linear transformations with an activation function between, applied positionally to the MHSA output: <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Z})=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>FFN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>ReLU</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Z})=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,  where <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{FFN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{FFN}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{FFN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{FFN}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{FFN}\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{FFN}\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}</annotation></semantics></math> are learnable parameters.
Each transformer encoder layer incorporates residual connections and layer normalization (LN), resulting in the output:
<math id="S2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{l}=\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}+\text{FFN}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}+\text{MSA}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}))))." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>LN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>FFN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>MSA</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{l}=\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}+\text{FFN}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1}+\text{MSA}(\mathbf{Z}_{l-1})))).</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">After passing through the <math id="S2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> transformer encoder layers, the final output sequence <math id="S2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}_{L}=[\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{L};\ldots;\mathbf{z}_{N}^{L}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐙</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}_{L}=[\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L};\mathbf{z}_{1}^{L};\ldots;\mathbf{z}_{N}^{L}]</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained. The output of the [CLS] token <math id="S2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is used for recognition by applying a linear transformation followed by softmax activation: <math id="S2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{cls}\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L}+\mathbf{b}_{cls})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{cls}\mathbf{z}_{cls}^{L}+\mathbf{b}_{cls})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times K}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}_{cls}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of classes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient ViT Components</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As the desire for improved image recognition precision continues to grow, challenges arise from image quality, object characteristics, and potential dependencies. The vision transformer stands out as particularly well suited for such tasks because of the unique representation advantages and robust adaptability to global understanding.
Consequently, novel designs for various components of ViT emerge in abundance, accompanied by additional training and inference costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the efforts towards online lightweight design of each component in the order in which it processes the input image within the network.
This includes <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding Structure Design</span> in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Position Encoding</span> in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. Efficient Position Encoding ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, <span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Token Update</span> in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. Efficient Token Update ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, and <span id="S3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Framework Design</span> in Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4. Framework Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span><span id="S3.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding Structure Design</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Patch embedding serves as the initial stage in the ViT pipeline, responsible for converting the input image into a sequence of tokens that can be processed by the transformer encoder. This stage plays a crucial role in determining the efficiency of the overall model, as the number of patches directly influences the computational complexity of subsequent self-attention layers.
Specifically, we discuss two prominent directions: <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Patch Partitioning (DPP)</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Local Patch Embedding (LPE)</span>.
DPP explores adaptive partitioning of the input image to generate effective patches at multiple scales and multiple views.
On the other hand, LPE leverages CNN models to extract rich local information.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2. </span>
A quantitative comparative analysis is conducted on the classic methods involved in <span id="S3.T2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding Structure Design</span> (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), using ImageNet-1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> as the benchmark, with the resolution standardized to <math id="S3.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224\times 224" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224\times 224</annotation></semantics></math>.
<sup id="S3.T2.5" class="ltx_sup">†</sup> denotes that the CrossViT model is modified by replacing the linear patch embedding in ViT with three convolutional layers as patch labelers.
The best-performing method is highlighted in bold, and the runner-up is underlined.
</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<td id="S3.T2.7.1.18.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1.6pt;padding-bottom:1.6pt;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.T2.pic34" class="ltx_picture" height="8.99" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 8.99 8.99" width="8.99"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#E0BE9F;--ltx-fill-color:#E0BE9F;--ltx-fg-color:#E0BE9F;" color="#E0BE9F" fill="#E0BE9F" stroke="#E0BE9F" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,8.99) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 8.99 L 8.99 8.99 L 8.99 0 Z M 8.99 8.99"></path></g></svg></span><span id="S3.T2.7.1.18.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">RepViT-M2.3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite></span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.7.1.18.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1.6pt;padding-bottom:1.6pt;"><span id="S3.T2.7.1.18.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">2024</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.7.1.18.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1.6pt;padding-bottom:1.6pt;"><span id="S3.T2.7.1.18.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">22.9</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.7.1.18.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1.6pt;padding-bottom:1.6pt;"><span id="S3.T2.7.1.18.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">9</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.7.1.18.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1.6pt;padding-bottom:1.6pt;"><span id="S3.T2.7.1.18.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">83.3</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div></div></div>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1. </span><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Patch Partitioning</span></h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DPP adapts to the computational demands by employing patches of varying sizes or dynamically adjusting patch dimensions. CrossViT<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/IBM/CrossViT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/IBM/CrossViT</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> employs a dual-branch Transformer with multi-scale patches, while SSA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2022</a>)</cite> merges tokens to represent larger objects efficiently. TopFormer<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/hustvl/TopFormer" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/hustvl/TopFormer</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> integrates multi-scale features using token and semantic pyramid modules, and T2T-ViT<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/yitu-opensource/T2T-ViT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/yitu-opensource/T2T-ViT</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2021</a>)</cite> adopts a hierarchical approach to model local structures. Dynamic patch partitioning techniques, such as IA-RED<sup id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">2</sup> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, DynamicViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rao et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, eliminate redundant or non-essential patches to optimize computational efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2. </span><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Local Patch Embedding</span></h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LPE incorporates convolutional layers into the patch embedding process, leveraging its local feature extraction capabilities while preserving the ViT global context understanding.
MobileViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehta and Rastegari, 2022</a>)</cite> uses convolutional layers to encode pixel information within non-overlapping patches.
MobileFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>)</cite> integrates a lightweight MobileNet, using global tokens to fuse local and global features.
CvT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> employs a hierarchical design with convolutional token embedding layers at each stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3. </span><span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary: Embedding Structure Design </span></h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The traditional global patch encoding strategy does not adequately capture local information from images, affecting the precision of fine-grained image recognition on ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, while a dense patch encoding approach incurs a higher computational burden. Two directions for improvement under this topic involve multi-scale and multi-perspective adaptive partitioning of input images, combined with CNNs to extract rich local features, enhancing the quality and efficiency of patch embedding. In Table  <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1. Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we report the relevant experimental results, where the following phenomena can be observed:
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(i).</span> The CrossViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> series introduces dynamic patch partitioning and local partition embedding mechanisms, significantly outperforming the traditional DeiT model, with competitive FLOPs and an accuracy improvement from <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81.0\%\rightarrow 82.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>81.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mn>82.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81.0\%\rightarrow 82.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>;
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(ii).</span> Lightweight variants such as
MobileViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehta and Rastegari, 2022</a>)</cite> and CvT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> achieve an excellent balance between accuracy and efficiency, for instance, MobileViT-S <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehta and Rastegari, 2022</a>)</cite> achieves an accuracy of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="78.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>78.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">78.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> with  just <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.6</annotation></semantics></math>M parameters;
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(iii).</span> State-of-the-art (SOTA) methods like SSA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and DPS-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> achieve a win-win in both accuracy and efficiency, with SSA-B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2022</a>)</cite> achieving a high accuracy of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="84.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>84.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">84.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> with only <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>39.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39.6</annotation></semantics></math>M parameters.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/picture/n1.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/138;" width="476" height="138" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4. </span>
<span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">How Positional Encoding Works.</span>
A comparative illustration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> of the vision transformer and its modified counterpart is presented. <math id="S3.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a)</annotation></semantics></math> depicts the ViT model that employs explicit learnable positional encodings. In contrast, <math id="S3.F4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b)</annotation></semantics></math> showcases the Conditional Positional Vision Transformer (CPVT) utilizing conditional positional encoding generated by the proposed Position Encoding Generator (PEG) plugin, which serves as the default configuration. <math id="S3.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(c)</annotation></semantics></math> illustrates the CPVT-GAP variant, which, in the absence of a [CLS] token, performs global average pooling (GAP) across all sequence elements.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span><span id="S3.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Position Encoding</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After converting the image input into a sequence of patches, it is necessary to encode the spatial information lost during patch partitioning.
This is where Position Encoding (PE) comes into play, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1.3. Summary: Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3.1. Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Traditional absolute positional encodings, such as the widely used sinusoidal method:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{PE}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\sin\left(\frac{\text{ pos }}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)&amp;\text{ if }&amp;i=2k\\
\cos\left(\frac{\text{ pos }}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)&amp;\text{ if }&amp;i=2k+1\end{array}\right." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>PE</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mtext> pos </mtext><msup><mn>10000</mn><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext> if </mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mtext> pos </mtext><msup><mn>10000</mn><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext> if </mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mphantom></mphantom></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{PE}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\sin\left(\frac{\text{ pos }}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)&amp;\text{ if }&amp;i=2k\\
\cos\left(\frac{\text{ pos }}{10000^{2k/d}}\right)&amp;\text{ if }&amp;i=2k+1\end{array}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1,\ldots,d/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1,\ldots,d/2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> denote the index and length of the vector respectively, and “pos” denotes the position of the element in the sequence.
While simple, this method suffers from limitations such as lack of adaptability to variable input sizes or non-available prior information.
Recent research has shifts towards more efficient and flexible position encoding techniques that can effectively capture spatial relationships while minimizing computational overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One promising direction is to incorporate relative positional information directly into the attention mechanism. RoPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heo et al., 2024</a>)</cite> achieves this by integrating query and key vectors, improving the ability of self-attention to encode spatial relationships. Similarly, PoSGU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> embeds positional information within the token mixing layer, maintaining expressiveness while reducing parameter overhead. Another approach leverages efficient computation methods for relative positional embeddings. LISA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2022</a>)</cite> employs the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to approximate relative positional embeddings, achieving log-linear complexity. FIRE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduces gradient interpolation techniques for relative encoding, and LRPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>)</cite> proposes efficient linear complexity encodings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, adapting positional encoding to varying input contexts shows significant promise. For example, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1.3. Summary: Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3.1. Embedding Structure Design ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, CPVT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> dynamically incorporate positional information by conditioning image patch content, thus enhancing model flexibility and performance. This is particularly beneficial for tasks such as extrapolating lengths in transformers, significantly improving medical segmentation tasks with Polyp-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sikkandar et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1. </span><span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary: Efficient Position Encoding</span></h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ViT is highly dependent on the self-attention mechanism for outstanding global understanding, which inherently lacks the ability to perceive the sequential or spatial relationships of the input data.
Effectively encoding positional information can enhance performance in several aspects:
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(i).</span> Facilitates the ViT model in comprehending the spatial structure of images, enabling it to differentiate objects and their positions within the frame, which is particularly crucial for ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, which contains a vast number of objects with diverse spatial configurations;
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(ii).</span> Allowing the ViT model to focus more effectively on relevant regions of the image;
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(iii).</span> Eliminates ambiguity in feature representations by ensuring that the position of each pixel or patch is known;
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(iv).<span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> </span></span> Accelerates the ViT model convergence speed during the training process by providing clear spatial signals, making the learning of large-scale image recognition datasets more reliable.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span><span id="S3.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Token Update</span></h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1. </span><span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Self-Attention</span></h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the spatial context re-introduced, the core component of the ViT architecture comes into play: Self-Attention (SA).
This mechanism empowers the model to capture long-range dependencies among patche inputs, enabling the comprehensive understanding of the image.
However, the computational complexity of standard self-attention grows quadratically with the number of tokens, posing a significant bottleneck for resource-constrained applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate this issue, researchers have made significant efforts to develop efficient self-attention mechanisms that maintain the ability of the model to capture global dependencies while reducing computational cost.
This section explores four prominent directions in efficient self-attention design: <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Partial Attention</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Local Self-Attention</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear Self-Attention</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Low-rank Decomposition</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/self-attention.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5. </span>
<span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Improvements in Self-Attention.</span>
CSwin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2022</a>)</cite> splits multi-heads (<math id="S3.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, …, <math id="S3.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>) into two groups and performs self-attention in horizontal and vertical stripes simultaneously. Then, CSwin adjusts the stripe width according to the network depth, which achieves a better trade-off between computational cost and capability.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.T3" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3. </span>
A quantitative comparative analysis is conducted on the classic methods involved in <span id="S3.T3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Self-Attention Optimization</span> (Section <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS1" title="3.3.1. Self-Attention ‣ 3.3. Efficient Token Update ‣ 3. Efficient ViT Components ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.1</span></a>), using ImageNet-1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> as the benchmark, with the resolution standardized to <math id="S3.T3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224\times 224" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224\times 224</annotation></semantics></math>.
The best-performing method is highlighted in bold, and the runner-up is underlined.
</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
