<figure id="S4.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/m1.png" id="S4.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/103;" width="333" height="103" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12. </span>
<span id="S4.F12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Early Exit Paradigm.</span>
Attaching additional internal classifiers at various stacked layers of the ViT model halts computation upon satisfying predefined exit conditions, thereby facilitating the early exit of simpler samples without compromising image recognition accuracy, which in turn conserves computational resources.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Dynamic multi-exit networks provide a flexible online lightweighting technique by enabling early computation halts.
AViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib196" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2022</a>)</cite> adapts ViT to dynamically adjust the depth and computation of the layer based on the specific task and the complexity of the input data.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib197" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phuong and Lampert, 2019</a>)</cite> enhances this paradigm using the knowledge distillation training procedure, allowing early exits to benefit from the abstract semantic knowledge of deeper layers.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 4.2. Depth Adaptation ‣ 4. Dynamic Network ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>,<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib198" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bakhtiarnia et al., 2022</a>)</cite> introduces a novel early exit architecture that uses fine-tuning to significantly improve exit accuracy. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib199" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bakhtiarnia et al., 2021</a>)</cite> integrates multi-exit architecture into ViT, proposing seven distinct early exit designs. To address performance degradation in early exit methods, LGViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib200" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> takes advantage of heterogeneous exit headers (local perceptual and global aggregation) to balance efficiency and precision.
DYN-ADAPTER<span id="footnote15" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">15</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/LMD0311/DAPT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/LMD0311/DAPT</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib201" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> dynamically adjusts the model capacity based on disentangled representations.
CF-ViT<span id="footnote16" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">16</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">16</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">16</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/ChenMnZ/CF-ViT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ChenMnZ/CF-ViT</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib178" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>)</cite> divides the processing pipeline into coarse and fine steps. AdaViT<span id="footnote17" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">17</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">17</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">17</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/MengLcool/AdaViT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/MengLcool/AdaViT</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib202" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2021</a>)</cite> adapts the depth adjustment of ViT models based on the complexity of the task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To further enhance the efficiency and adaptability of the ViT models, several dynamic training strategies are explored. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib203" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> presents a faster depth-adaptive transformer, taking advantage of dynamic adjustment of the model layers to optimize computational resources. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib204" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elbayad et al., 2020</a>)</cite> allows different layers to exit at different points, thus reducing unnecessary computations. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib205" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuster et al., 2022</a>)</cite> proposes a confident adaptive language model that dynamically halts computations based on confidence measures, which can be paralleled in vision tasks to enhance efficiency. Additionally, Skipdecode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib206" title="" class="ltx_ref">Corro et al., 2023</a>)</cite> presents an autoregressive skip decoding mechanism that can potentially be adapted for ViT models to optimize inference efficiency by skipping certain decoding steps while maintaining performance.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1. </span><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary: Depth Adaptation</span></h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In traditional fixed-depth networks, both simple and complex inputs undergo the same computational process, which to some extent wastes resources.
This topic introduces a dynamic multi-exit paradigm that allows the model to flexibly adjust its computational depth based on input complexity, which aligns with the principles of online lightweighting strategies.
The multi-exit structure can be regarded as a form of “implicit ensemble", where models of different depths share parameters but provide diverse decisions. Moreover, through knowledge distillation techniques, the early layers can also acquire deep semantic information. As ImageNet is a large-scale and inconsistent difficulty dataset, dynamic depth can offer better adaptability, improving overall recognition accuracy. For simple images, results can be obtained at shallower layers, reducing unnecessary computations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3. </span><span id="S4.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Networks Discussion</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the complexity of the input and the inherent token representation advantages of ViT, a wide variety of dynamic networks can be constructed.
Compared to the dynamic network paradigm of the CNN model, ViT has the additional advantage of handling input sequences of variable length. This means ViT does not need to worry about resizing to a rectangular space after eliminating redundancy, thus offering greater flexibility.
This flexibility is particularly beneficial in lightweight online strategies, where token pruning and merging are employed to reduce computational load while simultaneously enhancing recognition accuracy.
We report the relevant experimental results in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.1. Dynamic Resolution ‣ 4. Dynamic Network ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.1. Dynamic Resolution ‣ 4. Dynamic Network ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, and summarize the limitations of the existing methods as follows:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">a.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Lack of guidance for the pruning or merging layers, with the current widespread practice of manually setting them to be executed at the <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3^{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3^{th}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6^{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6^{th}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9^{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>9</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9^{th}</annotation></semantics></math> layers<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib195" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rao et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">b.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Adaptive pruning or merging rates, although learnable pruning rate methods such as DiffRate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib207" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite> are now available, require additional complex optimization techniques and training overhead.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">c.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Token pruning or token merging needs to be adapted to subsequent model pruning or quantization, making an end-to-end training strategy necessary.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">d.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although ViT can handle token sequences of variable lengths, token pruning or token merging disrupts position information, necessitating methods for re-modeling position information.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, for depth adaptation, the basic paradigm of the early exit strategy in CNN is generally followed, but the following limitations still exist:</p>
<ol id="S4.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">a.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Internal classifiers serve primarily as projections to category space, failing to fully leverage the advantage of token representations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">b.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Lack of effective guidance for the placement of internal classifiers.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">c.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The potential to skip individual components within transformer blocks, such as multi-head self-attention modules or feed-forward networks, rather than entire blocks.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F13" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/picture/n9.png" id="S4.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/280;" width="476" height="280" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13. </span>
<span id="S4.F13.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge Distillation Exploration Timeline.</span>
The figure collects and organizes the development of knowledge distillation methods in ViT model lightweighting. It includes two parts: feature knowledge distillation and response knowledge distillation.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge Distillation</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful approach to compress complex ViT models into lightweight and efficient variants suitable for image recognition tasks.
By extracting and transferring knowledge from a large, pre-trained teacher model to a smaller student model, knowledge distillation enables the creation of compact ViT architectures that maintain high accuracy while significantly reducing storage requirements and inference time.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib208" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hinton et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib209" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2021</a>)</cite> propose the concept of knowledge distillation, mainly focused on extracting class probability distributions through softening of labels.
In the context of lightweight online ViT strategies, knowledge distillation can be broadly categorized into two main topics: <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Feature Knowledge Distillation</span> in Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1. Feature Knowledge Distillation ‣ 5. Knowledge Distillation ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> and <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response Knowledge Distillation</span> in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2. Response Knowledge Distillation ‣ 5. Knowledge Distillation ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>.
In Figure <a href="#S4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ 4.3. Dynamic Networks Discussion ‣ 4. Dynamic Network ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, we summarize the timeline of significant explorations on these two topics.
It should be noted that the relation distillation, present in CNN models, remains applicable, while the relation distillation among tokens in ViT is more adapted.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1. </span><span id="S5.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Feature Knowledge Distillation</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Feature-based knowledge distillation (FKD) focuses on transferring rich intermediate-level information from a teacher model to a student model, capitalizing on the detailed representations within the internal layers of teacher networks.
FKD employs the multi-faceted strategy: <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attention Feature Distillation</span>, captures essential attention patterns, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured Feature Distillation</span>, compresses structural representations, and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Direct Feature Mimicking</span>, ensures that important features are transferred directly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">FKD emphasizes comprehensive guidance through intermediate feature information.
The typical loss function for feature-based distillation is defined as:</p>
<table id="S5.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S5.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_left">(3)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FKD}}(F^{S},F^{T})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{D}}(\phi^{S}(F^{S}),\phi^{T}(F^{T}))," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>FKD</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>D</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FKD}}(F^{S},F^{T})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{D}}(\phi^{S}(F^{S}),\phi^{T}(F^{T})),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the intermediate feature mappings from the student and teacher, respectively. The functions <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> transform these features to include enhanced information such as attention mechanisms, activation boundaries, neuron selectivity, and probability distributions. The loss function <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>D</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> measures the similarity between features, using metrics such as mean square error and Kullback-Leibler divergence.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.1.1. </span><span id="S5.SS1.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attention Feature Distillation</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Attention feature distillation transfers valuable information from teacher model attention maps.
AttnDistill <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib210" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> aligns class labels using the Projector Alignment (PA) module and approximates teacher network attention maps with the Attention Guidance (AG) module.
PFI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib211" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite> guides feature mimicry by emphasizing high-variance areas based on prediction variance.
ViT-FRD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib212" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2023</a>)</cite> refines knowledge transfer by integrating ViT and CNN using the Collaborative Reformer based on Clustering (CCReformer), the Linear Transformer (Linformer) as the knowledge distillation modules.
CFD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib213" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>)</cite> employs a dataset-independent classifier to distill the distribution of refined features to the student.
AFD<span id="footnote18" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">18</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">18</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">18</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/holger24/AFD" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/holger24/AFD</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib214" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2021</a>)</cite> takes advantage of attention-based meta-networks to control the strength of distillation by identifying similarities.
SAM-Net<span id="footnote19" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">19</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">19</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">19</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/benjaminkelenyi/SAM-Net" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/benjaminkelenyi/SAM-Net</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib215" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kelenyi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> dynamically adapts local features based on environmental and spatial correlations by exploiting cross-attention.
Attention Probe-Based Distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib210" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> selects significant real-world data and uses a probe knowledge distillation algorithm to train lightweight student models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/crop_x4.png" id="S5.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:310/195;" width="310" height="195" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14. </span>
<span id="S5.F14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Feature Knowledge Distillation Example</span>.
ViTKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib216" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> observes that regardless of model capacity, the attention gap in shallow layers is relatively small, advocating for a direct alignment strategy. In contrast, the attention distribution in deeper layers is more diverse, thus necessitating a generative alignment approach.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.1.2. </span><span id="S5.SS1.SSS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured Feature Distillation</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Structured feature distillation ensures effective knowledge transfer while maintaining structural integrity, which is crucial for lightweight vision transformers. Preserves and transfers structural information, helping student networks capture complex patterns and relationships, thus improving performance and generalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">KDFAS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib217" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> addresses the issue of embedding dimension gap by employing a covariance matrix during feature-level knowledge transfer, while DMKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib218" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employs a dual-attention mechanism to guide spatial and channel information to its respective masking branches and integrates reconstructed features.
PromptKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib219" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> transfers category embedding from teacher to student through shared distillation.
CrossKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib220" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> makes the student generate cross head predictions like the teacher.
MTKD-SSR<span id="footnote20" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">20</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">20</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">20</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/ChaofWang/Awesome-Super-Resolution" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ChaofWang/Awesome-Super-Resolution</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib221" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2023</a>)</cite> introduces the Staged Channel Distillation (SCD) mechanism, which takes advantage of channel attention to allow the student network to mimic the weight distribution within the channel feature map.
PSD<span id="footnote21" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">21</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">21</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">21</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/webtoon/psd" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/webtoon/psd</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib222" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> incorporates multiple self-distillations with a shared embedded network between the teacher and the student during each process, and TAKT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib223" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong et al., 2023</a>)</cite> proposes the Target-Aware Feature Alignment (TAFA) module to establish transferable feature connections between the source and target domains.
The cross-architecture knowledge distillation approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib224" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> aligns intermediate features using projectors for partial cross-attention and grouped linear transformations, while Fine-Grained Manifold Distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib225" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2022</a>)</cite> creates low-dimensional features by learning smooth manifolds embedded within the original feature space.
DearKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib226" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>)</cite> is a two-stage framework that initially refines the inductive bias from the early intermediate layers of the CNN, subsequently allowing the transformer to be fully leveraged through unrefined training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.1.3. </span><span id="S5.SS1.SSS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Direct Feature Mimicking</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diret Feature Mimicking alleviates the need for complex preprocessing of alignment targets, helping to preserve the native quality and inherent patterns of the information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib227" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ 5.1.1. Attention Feature Distillation ‣ 5.1. Feature Knowledge Distillation ‣ 5. Knowledge Distillation ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, ViTKD<span id="footnote22" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">22</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">22</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">22</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/yzd-v/cls_KD" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/yzd-v/cls_KD</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib216" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employs “linear layers" and “correlation matrices" for shallow tasks, a convolutional projector for deeper  generative tasks. MMKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib228" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> uses a meta-weighting network to integrate logic and intermediate features from various teacher models to guide the student network. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib229" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2022</a>)</cite> proposes a one-to-one spatial matching method that employs a target-aware transformer<span id="footnote23" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">23</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">23</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">23</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/Kevoen/TATrack" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Kevoen/TATrack</a></span></span></span> (TaT) to align the feature component.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.1.4. </span><span id="S5.SS1.SSS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary: Feature Knowledge Distillation</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To improve the performance of small capacity ViT models and facilitate their deployment in constrained environments, directly training compact ViT models often fails to achieve satisfactory performance, and simple knowledge distillation methods are insufficient to fully transfer the rich information embedded within the teacher model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, extracting the abundant latent patterns from the teacher network presents a promising direction.
Attention Feature Distillation enhances the ability of lightweight ViT models to identify critical information, while Structured Feature Distillation maintains the integrity of knowledge structures during the distillation process. Direct Feature Mimicking alleviates the burden of complex preprocessing.
This multifaceted feature knowledge distillation strategy effectively transfers the rich intermediate-layer information.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ 5.1.4. Summary: Feature Knowledge Distillation ‣ 5.1. Feature Knowledge Distillation ‣ 5. Knowledge Distillation ‣ Image Recognition with Online Lightweight Vision Transformer: A Survey" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, TinyMIM<span id="footnote24" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">24</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">24</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">24</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/OliverRensu/TinyMIM" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/OliverRensu/TinyMIM</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib230" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2023</a>)</cite> takes advantage of the unique representational advantages inherent in ViT architectures and
extracts relation knowledge among tokens as a complementary feature knowledge transfer, which differs from the conventional CNN approach of extracting relation knowledge among images within the input batch.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F15" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.03113v3/crop_x5.png" id="S5.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:310/201;" width="310" height="201" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15. </span>
<span id="S5.F15.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Token Relation Transfer.</span>
TinyMIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib230" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2023</a>)</cite> extracts the relation knowledge among tokens, including Q-K, V-V, K-K, and Q-Q, which differs from the conventional CNN of capturing the relation knowledge among images within the batch.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2. </span><span id="S5.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Response Knowledge Distillation</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Feature-based approaches recently come to the fore due to its superior performance in numerous applications. Consequently, response knowledge distillation (RKD) is relatively neglected. RKD, which facilitates direct learning from the output layer of the teacher model by the student model, presents distinct advantages, including rapid learning and straightforward implementation, and the potential remains largely unexplored. This outcome-driven approach makes it widely applicable across various tasks, given the recognition task, the soft probability distribution <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as:</p>
<table id="S5.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(4)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z_{i};T)=\frac{\exp(z_{i}/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(z_{j}/T)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z_{i};T)=\frac{\exp(z_{i}/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(z_{j}/T)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the logit for class <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of classes, and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is a temperature parameter controlling the distribution smoothness.
RKD aims to align the teacher probability distribution, <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z^{T};T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z^{T};T)</annotation></semantics></math>, with the student, <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z^{S};T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z^{S};T)</annotation></semantics></math>, by minimizing a distance function <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{dis}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{dis}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S5.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(5)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{RKD}=\mathcal{L}_{dis}\left(p(z^{S};T),p(z^{T};T)\right),y" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mi>S</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{RKD}=\mathcal{L}_{dis}\left(p(z^{S};T),p(z^{T};T)\right),y</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{dis}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{dis}</annotation></semantics></math> can be instantiated with various distance metrics, such as Kullback-Leibler divergence, mean squared error, or Pearson correlation. For example, the classic KD loss is formulated as:</p>
<table id="S5.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(6)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{RKD}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}p(z_{i}^{T};T)\log\frac{p(z_{i}^{T};T)}{p(z_{i}^{S};T)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>S</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{RKD}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}p(z_{i}^{T};T)\log\frac{p(z_{i}^{T};T)}{p(z_{i}^{S};T)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}^{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>S</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}^{S}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the teacher and student logits for class <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Improving response-based knowledge distillation can involve adjusting distillation <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temperature Variants</span> to transfer information-rich knowledge, optimizing <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> Objective Function Design</span> to diversify learning objectives, and <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empowering Soft Labels</span> to prevent overfitting.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.2.1. </span><span id="S5.SS2.SSS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temperature Variants</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Temperature variation by modulating the softness of the teacher model logit output, temperature scaling provides smoother and more informative probability distributions to the student model.
However, traditional fixed-temperature methods often fail to exploit the diverse properties of logit distributions across samples, leading to suboptimal knowledge transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib231" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome these limitations, there are several advanced techniques.
ATKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib232" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo, 2022</a>)</cite> dynamically adjusts the temperatures for both teacher and student outputs, balancing clarity and mitigating performance degradation.
MKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib233" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> introduces meta-learned temperature parameters that adapt throughout the training process based on the learning objective gradient.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib234" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2023</a>)</cite> introduces a multi-level logit distillation framework, which transforms them into multiple outputs with varying temperatures, and performs multi-level alignment matching.
NormKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib235" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al., 2023</a>)</cite> customizes the temperatures for each sample to achieve a uniform distribution by analyzing logit output.
SKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib236" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> integrates a temperature-scaled LogSoftmax function with a learning simplifyer to improve distillation loss during joint training.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib237" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite> propose using a weighted logit standard deviation as the adaptive temperature, combined with Z-score preprocessing to normalize logits before applying Softmax.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.2.2. </span><span id="S5.SS2.SSS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Objective Function Design</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Creative formulations of objective functions enhance the distillation process, allowing a wider variety of training for compact student models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Decoupled Knowledge Distillation (DKD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib238" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> splits KD loss into Target Class (TCKD) and Non-Target Class (NCKD) components, with NCKD weighting independent of teacher confidence.
Unified Self-Knowledge Distillation (USKD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib239" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> further refines the KD loss into target and non-target losses using cross-entropy, normalizes non-target logits to formulate the non-target knowledge distillation (NKD) loss, and generates customized soft labels to potentially improve knowledge transfer.
PTLoss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib240" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> represents the original KL-based distillation loss function through a maclaurin series and implicitly transforms the original teacher into a proxy teacher by perturbing the first-order term in this series.
NTCE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib241" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduces a Magnitude Kullback Leibler (MKL) divergence to better represent non-target categories, combined with diversity-based data augmentation (DDA) to enrich non-target category diversity.
CSKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> terminates the pooling operation following the final feature map, producing dense predictions for each corresponding feature location. From these results, hard labels are derived to serve as target labels, utilizing cross-entropy as the loss function for spatial knowledge transfer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.2.3. </span><span id="S5.SS2.SSS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empowering Soft Labels</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reducing the influence of the teacher model in knowledge distillation seeks to create vision transformer models that are more lightweight and autonomous. This approach moves away from a strong reliance on pre-trained teachers, allowing students to learn on their own.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The Tf-KD framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib242" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2020</a>)</cite> replaces dark knowledge with the model own predictions, using self generated soft targets for regularization, and achieves smoothing effects similar to label smoothing regularization (LSR).
MTKDSSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib221" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2023</a>)</cite> incorporates staged channel distillation, staged response distillation, and cross-stage distillation, using student self-reflection through self-distillation of response-based knowledge.
The OFA-KD framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib243" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> eliminates architecture-specific information and employs exit branches in the student model trained with teacher model logits.
MEKD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib244" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite> transitions from logits to cell boundaries, innovating with de-privatization and distillation for lightweight model transformations.
WTTM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib245" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng and Yang, 2024</a>)</cite> enhances the training of the student model using sample-adaptive weighting to emulate the power-transformed probability distributions of the teacher. Tiny-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib246" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> focuses on reducing memory and computational overhead through logit sparsification and efficient knowledge transfer during pre-training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.2.4. </span><span id="S5.SS2.SSS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary:Response Knowledge Distillation</span></h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Response knowledge distillation enhances efficiency, prevents overfitting, and facilitates cross-architecture knowledge sharing due to its flexible implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib247" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
We cover three topics: Temperature Variants exploit logit distribution characteristics better than fixed temperature methods; Objective Function Design diversifies learning objectives for more comprehensive knowledge transfer; Empowering Soft Labels lessens dependence on pre-trained teacher models, enhancing student models independent learning.
Furthermore,
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(i).</span> Response knowledge distillation provides soft guidance, offering richer information than hard labels.
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(ii).</span> Given the prevalent long-tail issue in image recognition tasks, leveraging the teacher model performance on rare categories to improve the student model’s learning can be achieved by adjusting the response distillation loss weight to focus on rare categories.
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">(iii).</span> Provides a lightweight response-based multi-scale knowledge transfer pathway <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib248" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, distinctly different from the burdensome multi-scale feature knowledge distillation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3. </span><span id="S5.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge Distillation Discussion</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge distillation bridges CNN and ViT models for cross-structural knowledge transfer. We focus on KD strategies that take advantage of both, especially ViT. For example, AttnDistill <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib210" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> uses the importance distribution between the [CLS] token and the image tokens to achieve a more efficient alignment of the target. ViT models effectively extract relevant knowledge for tasks in response knowledge distillation.
TinyMIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib230" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2023</a>)</cite> adapts the popular relation knowledge transfer in CNN to ViT using Q-K, V-V, K-K, and Q-Q relationships among tokens.
We summarize the limitations of existing methods as follows:</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">a.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exploiting the unique structural advantages of ViT for knowledge distillation, including head-level distillation, where existing methods still involve numerous artificial settings or task-coupling characteristics.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">b.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The fast distillation direction, focusing on response knowledge distillation, can be extended to feature knowledge distillation and even combined with self-supervised optimization objectives.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">c.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Addressing privacy and security concerns during the knowledge distillation process as well as enhancing the robustness of the student network in abnormal scenarios post-distillation.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Future Research Directions</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision transformer models excel in computer vision, but their high parameter and computational needs hinder their practical use.
Future lightweight ViT models will emphasize efficiency, intelligence, and security.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Representation Advantage Expansion.</span> Breaking free of the limitations of static model structures, the focus shifts from the previous global perspective to a more fine-grained local perspective, while integrating the unique representational advantages of ViT, such as deep adaptability and response knowledge distillation, which remain directions worthy of profound exploration in their ingenious integration with ViT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">End-to-End Training System.</span>
Offline lightweight ViT techniques, such as post-training quantization, remain relatively independent of online lightweight techniques. Future exploration can focus on designing end-to-end training systems, where errors arising from token pruning and merging can also be perceived and controlled.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Automatic Configuration.</span>
Existing online lightweight strategies for ViT still involve a significant number of scenarios that require manual intervention. We advocate for the automation of these processes, focusing primarily on two aspects:</p>
<ol id="S6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">a.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Analysis of performance bottlenecks and selection of the corresponding combination strategies can be automated by structuring the pipeline.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">b.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Within specific strategies, manually set parameters, such as the location of the layer and the corresponding rate, remain for token pruning and merging.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Privacy-Sensitive Lightweight.</span>
Traditional knowledge distillation requires access to the original training dataset, which may not be feasible in privacy-sensitive application scenarios. Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) methods generate synthetic data using only the teacher model, without accessing the original data, thus protecting data privacy. However, DFKD has not yet been explored in the ViT domain. We offer several valuable research directions:</p>
<ol id="S6.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">a.</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using the diffusion vision transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib249" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib250" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> instead of the CNN generator to transfer knowledge on synthetic datasets that better match real data distributions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">b.</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The current DFKD setup <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib251" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2024</a>)</cite> still reveals the original dataset input resolution to the user, and using the flexible ViT input form can enhance the benefits of the data-free paradigm.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S6.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inference Security.</span>
Well-trained teacher networks possess greater robustness against anomalous inputs, but the lightweight optimization process of the ViT model does not explicitly transfer this knowledge. This makes small ViT models more susceptible to adversarial attacks. Consequently, the extraction and transfer of robust, interference-resistant knowledge is a crucial consideration for future practical deployments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7. </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conclusion</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive investigation into lightweight techniques for vision transformer in image recognition, with particular emphasis on online lightweight strategies.
Our exploration is divided into three key topics: vision transformer <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Component Design</span>, <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Network</span>, and <span id="S7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge Distillation</span>.
We analyze these lightweight approaches both quantitatively and qualitatively in terms of the trade-offs between precision and efficiency, under the consistent view on ImageNet-1K.
For each topic, we present the methods in the form of input flow forward the network, allowing flexible component combinations and bottleneck identification.
In addition, we discuss the limitations of related explorations within each topic and propose potential solutions. However, numerous unknown challenges remain in the face of complex real-world scenarios, thus advocate for maintaining the privacy and security of the lightweighting process to ensure the broad acceptance and usage of ViT.
In summary, we hope that this survey will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, providing insight and guidance for the development of lightweight vision systems.</p>
</div>
</section>

      all.</p>
